sections.blurb: Read this tab first. Everything else is detail.
sections.title: How to Qualify

blocks.content:
You design a hook. Your teammate designs a hook. The two of you enter a double elimination bracket where hooks are pulled **against each other** on the rig until one breaks.

The hook that breaks loses. The hook that survives moves on with whatever damage it took. Your team is out when both of your hooks are gone.

This guide is the rulebook. A hook that misses any requirement in Dimensions or Manufacturing does not enter the bracket. Everything else in here is advice, and the advice is what decides who wins.
![Fig 07. Hooks from four previous tournaments. Nearly every one failed in the same place.](attachment:HOOK_FIG07_Break_Wall.png)

blocks.title: The rule behind every other rule
blocks.content: You can be asked to explain any part of your design, in your own words, at any time. A dimension you cannot justify gets corrected before the work earns credit. That is a correction, not a penalty.

sections.blurb: Checked at inspection. A miss is a disqualification, not a deduction.
sections.title: Dimensions

rows.requirement: 2.000 in to 2.500 in between the centres of the two 0.75 in features.
One 0.750 in diameter closed hole or loop.
A minimum 0.750 in clear opening extending all the way to the edge.
60.0 g, measured on the scale after printing.

blocks.title: The slide-in requirement
blocks.content: The hook side must be shaped so a standard 0.75 in diameter cylinder slides straight into the throat from the outside, with no interference. One physical go gauge checks both openings at inspection.

### Tolerancing

A 0.750 in opening modelled in CAD will usually come out tight in the printed part. Use your test hooks to find how much you need to oversize it in SolidWorks. Do not guess it once and print the real thing.

### Mass

The number that counts is the one on the scale, not the one in CAD or the slicer. Leave yourself a buffer. A part at 59.8 g in Bambu Studio is not a part at 59.8 g on the bench.

### Thickness

You have a full inch now. That is a lot of material to spend, and spending all of it everywhere puts you over 60 g before you have done anything clever. Thickness is a tool you use where the stress is, not a default.

blocks.title: Retractable hook allowance
blocks.content: A closed-loop design such as a carabiner-style gate is permitted on the hook side, provided a 0.75 in cylinder can pass into the throat when the mechanism is fully opened. The mechanism must be non-permanent and integral to the hook. It must be secured and actuated within 10 seconds at technical inspection.

sections.title: V1 to V3

blocks.title: V3 gets the extra time on purpose
blocks.content: Simulation and scale testing repeat as many times as you can manage. Class time gates the checkpoints. The shop is open from 7:30, at lunch, and until 4:30 for the iterating. The students who place well are the ones who use it.

sections.blurb: What matters is a finished, functional, legal hook.
sections.title: Design and CAD

blocks.content:
There is no CAD etiquette requirement in this project. Sketches do not have to be fully defined. Fixed geometry is allowed. Your design tree does not have to be organised or renamed.

Model it however you can get it done. What is graded is whether the hook is finished, functional, and legal, and whether you can explain the decisions in it.

### Make it interesting anyway

A blocky hook is a weak hook, and that is a structural claim rather than an aesthetic one. Sharp corners concentrate stress and flat slabs waste mass. Splines, variable fillets, and cut-out patterns produce shapes that are lighter and stronger at the same time, and they happen to look better.

blocks.title: Effort is protected
blocks.content: A complex design showing real design intent is protected from small non-structural modelling errors that would sink a simpler part. Ambition is not punished here. Reach past what you know how to do.

sections.blurb: Three ways it ends. One of them is almost always yours.
sections.title: Where Hooks Break

blocks.content: Every hook in the box behind you came out of a previous tournament, and they fail in a small number of ways. Learn to recognise them now and you will design around them instead of discovering them in September.
![Fig 04. Fractured at the inside corner of the throat. The most common failure by a wide margin.](attachment:HOOK_FIG04_Break_Throat.png)

### The throat, inside corner

This is where the load path turns a corner, and a sharp corner concentrates stress into a line rather than spreading it across material. It is the single most common failure in this competition.

A generous fillet here buys more strength per gram than anything else you can do to the part.
![Fig 05. Fractured through the anchor. Usually a hook that was too thin around the hole.](attachment:HOOK_FIG05_Break_Anchor.png)

### Through the anchor

Usually a hook that spent its mass on the hook end and left too little material around the anchor hole. Both ends carry the same force. Both ends need material.
![Fig 06. Deformed and pulled open instead of snapping. It did not break; it stopped being a hook.](attachment:HOOK_FIG06_Break_Pullthrough.png)

### Pulled open

It did not snap. It bent until the throat opened and the other hook slid out. Under the rules this is a loss exactly like a fracture, because you no longer have a hook.

This one is deceptive: a part that deforms instead of breaking often looks strong right up until it stops holding anything.

blocks.title: Which of these is yours?
blocks.content: You will not know until you run a simulation and then break a half-scale print. That is what V2 and V3 are for, and it is why the phase is built the way it is.

sections.blurb: A hook that cannot be printed well is not a good design.
sections.title: Designing for the Printer

blocks.content: Your part is printed flat on the plate, so its whole outline is the print cross section. That removes most overhang problems and replaces them with a different set. These are design decisions, made in CAD, before you ever open the slicer.

rows.fix: Keep structural features wide enough to slice as solid walls, then confirm it in the slicer preview rather than assuming.
rows.issue: Thin features do not slice the way you drew them. A narrow rib can come out as two walls with a gap down the middle, or as one wall, or as nothing at all.

rows.fix: Fillet every internal corner. This is the cheapest strength you will ever buy.
rows.issue: Sharp internal corners are both a stress riser and a place the toolpath leaves a void.

rows.fix: Round the outside corners of your outline rather than leaving points, and glue the plate.
rows.issue: Large flat parts curl off the plate at their corners as they cool.

rows.fix: Keep the part one connected mass in the plane of the plate.
rows.issue: Islands. A feature that starts mid-air, unconnected to anything below it, has nothing to print onto.

rows.fix: Model the openings oversize by whatever your test hooks tell you, not by whatever seems reasonable.
rows.issue: A part that only barely fits the constraints leaves you nothing when the print comes out slightly small.

columns.label: What you do about it in CAD

blocks.title: Look at the sliced preview before you commit
blocks.content: Step through the layer preview and look at where the walls actually go. Three hours of print time is a lot to spend on a part nobody looked at in the slicer. This is also where you find out that the rib you thought was structural is hollow.

sections.blurb: A diagnostic that tells you where. It does not tell you how much.
sections.title: Simulation

blocks.title: Set the material to Nylon 101, not to a HIPS or ABS entry
blocks.content: SolidWorks is poorly conditioned for ABS-family polymers and will not give you a usable study. In a single-material part under a fixed load, the stress pattern barely depends on which material you pick, so the hot spot you find with Nylon 101 is the hot spot your HIPS part actually has.

rows.value: The upper internal face of the anchor hole.
400 lbf tensile, on the inner radius of the hook opening.

blocks.content:
### What you read off the plot

**Location.** Where is the red. That is where your hook will break.

**Relative magnitude.** How much worse is the throat than the shank. That tells you where material is worth adding and where it is worth removing.

### What you do not read off the plot

Factor of safety, displacement, and predicted failure load. Those numbers are wrong here because the material is a stand-in, and quoting one in your write-up is a mistake rather than a shortcut.

The honest division of labour across the whole project: **the simulation tells you where, the scale test tells you whether your geometry survived contact with a printer, and the rig tells you how much.**

blocks.title: AI is unrestricted for the software
blocks.content: There is no limit on AI help for driving SolidWorks in this project. Paste the assistant prompt from Your SolidWorks Assistant and ask it anything about the program, as often as you like. The one thing it will not do is make your design decisions, because those are the part you have to defend out loud.

sections.blurb: HIPS on the X1C and the H2D. You run your own prints.
sections.title: Manufacturing

rows.rule: Provided HIPS only. Any colour on the shelf.
The provided Generic ABS profile. You do not set filament or temperature parameters.
Flat on the build plate. Mandatory. This runs the grain along the length of the hook.
The balance of wall loops against infill density. This is the real slicer lesson.
Glue the plate. Do it every few prints, not once a month.

blocks.title: Perimeters carry the load
blocks.content: In an FDM part most of the strength is in the walls, not the infill. A hook with thin walls and dense infill is heavy and weak, which is the worst combination available to you. Spend your 60 g where it works.

### What the scale test can and cannot tell you

A half-scale hook has a quarter of the cross section, but the wall thickness does not scale with it. The test part is proportionally more wall than the real one, so it is stronger than the geometry alone predicts.

**Failure location transfers. Failure load does not.** Use the test hook to confirm where it breaks and whether it printed the way you drew it. Do not use its number to predict what the full-size part will hold.

sections.blurb: Hook against hook. One rig. One hook dies per match.
sections.title: Tournament Rules

blocks.content:
### The match

Two hooks are linked in the load path and pulled against each other on the rig. The first to break loses the match. Exactly one hook is destroyed per match.

The winning hook advances **with its damage**. It has been loaded near failure and it is not the part it was. That is part of the game.

### Your team's decision

You hold two hooks and each round you choose which one to send. If they are different designs, that choice is a real bet: send the strong one now, or hold it for the losers bracket. If they are identical, the choice is about damage instead, a fresh hook against the veteran that has already survived two pulls. Either way it is a decision, and it decides more matches than you would think.

### Elimination

Double elimination. Two losses puts your team out, which is exactly two dead hooks. A team is never eliminated while it still holds a hook.

rows.detail: Hooks are weighed on a precision scale after printing. 60.0 g is the ceiling.
Over 60.0 g, you remove material by hand until it is legal. Drill, file, sand. No reprints for an overweight part.
Provided HIPS only. No screws, tape, glue, or any external reinforcement.
A team that brings two legal hooks enters the double elimination bracket. A team with one hook enters single elimination and is out on its first loss.
Your two hooks may be the same design or two different ones. Both are legal strategies.
Any gate or retractable mechanism must be secured and actuated within 10 seconds at inspection.

Designs must be your own. Copying a known public design, including the Tom Stanton Polymaker hook or a hook from a previous rotation, is a disqualification. Studying them for ideas is encouraged and expected.
The winner is the last team holding an intact hook. A team coming out of the losers bracket must break through the top team's remaining hooks to take the title.
The champion hook never breaks in the bracket, so it has no number. It gets pulled to failure at the close with everyone watching. That number goes on the wall.

blocks.title: Safety at the rig
blocks.content: Eye protection on everyone in the room, no exceptions. HIPS snaps and it throws pieces, so stand back far enough that a broken hook is not your problem. Use your head.

sections.blurb: Run this on your own hook before you bring it. Nothing here is a surprise.
sections.title: Inspection Checklist

blocks.content:
Every item is pass or fail. A fail does not enter the bracket.

1. Printed in the provided HIPS.
2. Mass on the scale is 60.0 g or under.
3. Thickness is 1.00 in or under.
4. The 0.75 in go gauge passes through the anchor hole.
5. The 0.75 in go gauge slides into the hook throat from the outside, with no interference.
6. Centre-to-centre distance measures between 2.000 in and 2.500 in.
7. No screws, tape, glue, or external reinforcement anywhere on the part.
8. Any gate mechanism secures and actuates inside 10 seconds.
9. The design is your own.

blocks.title: Check your own part the night before
blocks.content: Every item on this list can be checked at open shop with the gauge and the scale sitting on the bench. A hook that fails inspection on tournament day failed it days earlier and nobody looked.
